headline: High-risk data leakage and cascading-error concerns: EMQX’s broad egress can expose outputs while awesome-nlp provides no isolation or verification path.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared communication channel, filesystem, or clipboard bridge is documented between awesome-nlp and EMQX. awesome-nlp is non-runnable and EMQX only exposes an HTTP API, so a prompt-injection pathway is not evidenced from the profiles alone.
conditions: IF a shared filesystem, clipboard, or MCP bridge is added between the agents, injection risk becomes plausible.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate hosts or containers.
Do not pipe EMQX output into awesome-nlp as instructions.
Disable any shared clipboard or shared workspace mounts.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging if a bridge is introduced.

B_data_leakage.rationale: EMQX has broad network egress and touches IoT data, while awesome-nlp has no documented isolation or data-handling controls. If any shared workspace or copied content includes sensitive material, EMQX can transmit it outward; the pairwise leakage path is plausible even though the exact bridge is undocumented.
conditions: IF the two agents share files, pasted text, or an operator workspace containing sensitive data, leakage becomes possible.
IF EMQX is allowed to send its context to external endpoints, exposed content can leave the environment.
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of any shared workspace.
Run EMQX behind an egress allowlist.
Separate operator accounts for each agent.
Review logs for copied payloads before enabling sharing.
requires-engineering: add DLP or redaction on shared inputs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-nlp is non-runnable and has no write surfaces, while EMQX exposes HTTP API access but no filesystem or git write capability is documented. That makes direct capability overlap small; any conflict would require extra orchestration not shown in either profile.
conditions: IF an orchestrator grants both agents write access to the same mutable resource, conflict risk increases.
IF EMQX is configured to mutate shared state through its HTTP API, overlap may matter.
mitigations: Avoid giving both agents the same writable directory.
Do not share mutable git or database state.
Use separate service accounts.
Lock any shared resource before writes.
requires-engineering: add concurrency control for shared APIs.

D_cascading_error.rationale: EMQX can act on HTTP API inputs, so if awesome-nlp outputs are forwarded into EMQX without verification, bad text can cascade into downstream actions. The profiles do not show a built-in validation step, so the safer assumption is that the handoff is untrusted.
conditions: IF awesome-nlp output is used as authoritative input to EMQX workflows, cascading errors are possible.
IF no human or rule-based verification step exists between the agents, the risk increases.
mitigations: Insert a manual review step before forwarding outputs.
Require schema validation on all handoffs.
Limit EMQX actions to dry-run mode first.
Log and compare outputs against source data.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates.

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data and has broad egress, while awesome-nlp is an open-source repo with no residency or retention controls documented. If regulated IoT or personal data flows through the pair, the mismatch in handling and logging expectations can create compliance gaps; the profiles do not prove a specific violation, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data or personal data is routed through EMQX, compliance review is required.
IF retention or residency requirements apply and are not configured, the gap becomes material.
mitigations: Classify the data before routing it.
Disable unnecessary logging.
Restrict EMQX to approved regions.
Document retention settings.
requires-engineering: implement residency and deletion controls.
